newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Thyssen, Veba deny Vulkan report.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thyssen, Veba deny Vulkan report.

text.p: German industrial groups Thyssen AG and Veba AG denied the top story in a leading business daily on Wednesday that they were interested in taking over bankrupt shipyard group Bremer Vulkan Verbund AG.

The Duesseldorf-based daily Handelsblatt said on its front page the two companies, while distancing themselves from takeover speculation, wanted to pick up loss carryovers totalling three to four billion marks to cut their tax exposure.
Veba said in a statement, "Veba sharply denies newspaper reports that it is interested in a takeover of Bremer Vulkan AG...There is absolutely nothing in it."
Thyssen had on Tuesday denied a report in the Weser Kurier, a Bremen newspaper, that it wanted to buy Vulkan.
Equities analysts found the possibility of a takeover intriguing, but said it would be legally difficult.
"The tax-loss carry-forwards are certainly an asset for a potential buyer. Vulkan wasn't able to make use of them because of a lack of profit," said analyst Olaf Toelke at Merrill Lynch in London.

The Handelsblatt report said Thyssen, which is pursuing a strategy to refocus on its core steel and engineering, was planning to sell its E-Plus mobile telephone unit -- a move which would lead to sizeable extraordinary earnings.

To cut its tax exposure, Thyssen could offset the windfall gain from the E-Plus sale by offsetting it with the Vulkan loss carryover. Telecommunications venture o.tel.o, which is owned by utilities Veba and RWE AG, has been named as a potential buyer for E-Plus.
But Toelke said German law would only allow the Vulkan losses to be used to offset German domestic operating profits, and probably only in the shipbuilding or machinery sectors.

A buyer would need to negotiate with tax authorities for permission to use the losses to offset extraordinary gains, but that would appear extremely unlikely in this case given the German government's current fiscal straits and the background of the Bremer Vulkan collapse.
"It would be asking the authorities to subsidise the Bremer Vulkan losses a second time," Toelke said.

The Handelsblatt quoted informed sources saying that the two potential buyers wanted to dampen takeover talk to prevent shares in Bremer Vulkan -- which are still listed -- from jumping further after their price trebled on Monday.
Bremer Vulkan shares were trading on Wednesday at 7.40 marks, up from Tuesday's close of 5.10 marks. On Monday they had surged to 9.90 marks from 3.44 marks last Friday.

That is still a far fall from the level of around 80 marks where they were trading a year ago. The Bremen shipbuilder collapsed after it emerged that managers had misused European Union industrial subsidies to prop up the company.

Ulrich Noelle, finance senator for the city state, confirmed at the weekend that he was talking to two potential buyers. Handelsblatt said in its report, however, that Noelle had distanced himself from such plans.
One member of the committee of creditors to Vulkan, Joerg Stein, told Handelsblatt that a sale of the group to the two potential buyers would be "sensible, wise and achievable".
